description: Curious to explore space and matter in every form
summary:
ORBITWELL is a single-file web app that helps monitor astronaut health, combining three modules into one workflow. The first module, Pulsefield, tracks heart rate from a live or demo stream, showing current rate, average, variation and trend. The second, a diagnostic console, collects radiation, respiratory, blood, urine, sleep and cardiac readings, then analyses them into an overall status, a 0–100 health score and findings with recommended protocols. It offers a 3D anatomy view, per-crew history logs, a procedures manual and PDF export.

After the analysis is saved, the app hands the crew member over to the third module, a private 45-question psychological wellness check-in adapted from the techy-tej NASA-astro-psychometric repository. Its first screen asks whether someone is in an emergency; if so, the questions are skipped and a report is produced immediately, with photo capture and a live preview.

Both the emergency and normal reports include the heart-monitor and console data. Nothing from the check-in is stored, and sharing never happens automatically. Everything runs in the browser from one HTML file, with no server or account needed, so setup takes seconds.
details:
What it does and how it works
ORBITWELL is a health-monitoring app for astronauts that joins three steps into one flow. First, a heart monitor (Pulsefield) tracks heart rate, average, variation and trend. Second, a diagnostic console takes radiation, respiratory, blood, urine, sleep and cardiac readings, and analyses them into an overall status, a 0–100 health score, and findings with recommended protocols. It also has a 3D anatomy view, per-crew history logs and a procedures manual. Third, once the physical analysis is saved, the crew member is moved straight into a private 45-question psychological wellness check-in. If someone is in an emergency, that screen skips the questions and produces a report immediately, with photo capture. Both the emergency and normal reports include the heart and diagnostic data, ready to share with a flight surgeon.

Benefits
Crews get physical and mental health in one place instead of separate tools. The emergency path gives a flight surgeon the full picture within seconds, when a crew member has no time for a questionnaire. Trends in the history logs help catch gradual changes early.

Intended impact
Earlier detection of health risks on long missions such as Mars transit or lunar operations, where medical help is delayed. It also normalises routine mental-health check-ins and makes it easier for crewmates to report an emergency.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript in a single offline-capable file, with canvas for the charts and 3D anatomy. The check-in logic comes from an open-source TypeScript project, bundled with esbuild. We also used the browser’s camera, Web Share and local storage features. No special hardware is needed. The heart monitor accepts a live heart-rate feed or a built-in demo stream.

Creativity
It merges separate tools into one handoff and puts the emergency shortcut first in the final step. Everything runs in the browser from one file with no server or account, and check-in answers and photos are never stored.

Factors our team considered
Privacy, since sensitive health data stays on the device. Speed in emergencies, safety wording that never replaces contacting mission control, and the limits of spaceflight: no internet, delayed medical support and long mission durations.
